title: runtime-hooks-incremental-parse-and-schema-enforcement
content:
Context and motivation:

We need to make tool/function-calling hooks in the runtime robust for production traffic where structured-output expectations (JSON, proto-ish maps, typed records) are enforced while preserving latency and caching benefits. Current experiments show two recurring failure modes: (1) model returns syntactically invalid JSON or includes additional commentary that breaks downstream parsers, and (2) cached responses are reused in contexts where ephemeral fields (timestamps, request_ids) cause subtle correctness bugs.

Goals:
- Define a hook contract that allows the runtime to (a) detect/repair common structured-output failures, (b) decide when to validate strictly vs accept lax outputs, and (c) safely interact with KV cache and batching/scheduler so we don't regress latency or cache hitrates.
- Provide recommended JSON modes and a small set of canonical transform/repair behaviours the runtime can apply before handing the output to function-call plumbing.
- Specify constraints for kernel-level decisions (determinism, sampling temperature) that affect structured output reliability.
- Document lifecycle and idempotency requirements so cached results are safe when function-calls or side-effects are involved.

Design principles (high level):
- Fail closed for side-effecting tool calls: if the hook cannot confidently parse/validate the structure required for a side-effect (DB write, external API call), return an explicit parsing error instead of attempting a best-effort repair.
- Fail open for read-only tooling where graceful degradation is acceptable (e.g., best-effort metadata extraction).
- Keep repairs minimal and auditable: any automatic transform must include metadata indicating repair type and confidence so downstream owners can triage regressions.
- Keep latency budget in mind: do light-weight repairs in the hot path; schedule heavier repairs (full-sanitization, external schema validation) off the GPU thread pool.

JSON modes (runtime-level):
1) strict-json: Model output must be a single well-formed JSON value (object/array/primitive). Any additional tokens before/after JSON cause parse failure. Use for side-effecting calls and high-SLO endpoints.
2) permissive-json: Allow extra surrounding text, multiple top-level JSON snippets; runtime will attempt to extract the first top-level JSON blob. Useful for telemetry/exploratory workloads.
3) incremental-json: For streaming responses, the runtime will parse as streaming chunks and attempt progressive validation of the partial document; on finalization it must revalidate complete JSON. Good for long sequences with streaming tools.
4) schema-anchored-json: Accepts a JSON Schema id/reference. Runtime will validate and can optionally attempt auto-cast (e.g., numeric strings -> numbers) for a small safe set of casts. Use only when schema supplied and endpoint allows auto-cast.

Hook API sketch (conceptual fields exposed to runtime):
- mode: one of strict-json | permissive-json | incremental-json | schema-anchored-json
- schema_ref: optional string (schema id)
- repair_policy: one of none | minimal | aggressive (explained below)
- side_effects_allowed: boolean (if false, cached results may be returned without extra check)
- max_repair_time_ms: integer (budget for repairs on hot path)
- audit_labels: list[string] (tags included on any repaired/validated response)

Repair policies (behavioural):
- none: do no repair; parse-only, return parse errors upstream.
- minimal: apply fast deterministic fixes: strip leading/trailing non-JSON text, balance simple unbalanced braces/brackets heuristics (only if trivial), remove trailing commas, convert top-level single backtick-wrapped content. Always attach repair metadata.
- aggressive: attempt more costly heuristics and normalization (join split strings, try common markdown/code fences removal, try simple CSV->JSON mapping heuristics). Aggressive repairs may be deferred to background tasks depending on max_repair_time_ms.

Metadata added to responses when repairs/validation occur:
- runtime_hook.repaired: "true"|"false"
- runtime_hook.repair_steps: [list of short strings]*
- runtime_hook.validation: "ok"|"schema_mismatch"|"parse_error"|"partial"
- runtime_hook.repair_confidence: "high"|"medium"|"low"
- runtime_hook.processing_time_ms: numeric-as-string
(Implementation note: metadata should be added as separate envelope fields the application can opt out of; do not mutate the canonical payload unless the caller explicitly requests in-place normalization.)

KV cache interactions and invariants:
- Cache keys should be computed from normalized request context + hook mode + schema_ref + relevant routing tags. Example key: sha256(text_normalized+mode+schema_ref+route_tier).
- Cached payloads must carry the same runtime_hook.* metadata so callers can make decisions based on how the response was produced.
- Never serve cached responses for requests that declare side_effects_allowed=false if the cached value indicates it was produced with side_effects in the original context (need per-entry side_effects provenance).
- Ephemeral fields: when the model includes fields that are explicitly marked ephemeral (e.g., request_id, generated_at), runtime must either strip them before caching or store a template plus ephemeral-substitutions. Prefer to strip before caching unless caller used a flag keep_ephemeral_for_cache.
- Cache invalidation rules: entries pinned by model-version, prompt-hash, and schema_ref only. If schema evolves (schema id mapping change), old cached entries are invalidated. Consider a soft TTL for permissive repairs so we can re-run strict validation periodically.

Scheduler/Batching considerations:
- Hooks that perform heavy parsing/repairs should be scheduled off the GPU thread to a CPU worker pool. Keep hot-path parsing to minimal deterministic steps.
- Provide a hook priority hint: {latency_sensitive, balanced, throughput} so scheduler can decide between immediate single-request processing vs batching.
- When batching is used, validation/repair must be applied per-response; batching only applies to forward LLM token generation. Repairs are pure CPU-bound post-processing and should not hold batch slots.
- Streaming + incremental-json: scheduler must be able to emit partial tokens to the client while also running incremental-parse validators; if a partial validation fails irrecoverably, emit a structured error message and close stream gracefully.

Kernel/Model-level constraints impacting structured outputs:
- Determinism vs sampling: structured output reliability increases as sampling temperature approaches 0; for strict-json mode recommend temperature <= 0.2 and top_p <= 0.8 depending on model. Dedicated config should allow overriding at route level.
- KV cache reuse: cached KV should only be reused when the model variant and generation config are compatible. Kernels that alter tokenization or beam/fastgen heuristics must mark cache compatibility bitmask in the cache metadata.
- Quantization and small kernels may change numeric formatting (e.g., exponent notation differences). When schema requires precise numeric forms (strings vs numbers), document these caveats and prefer schema-anchored-json for numeric coercions.

Edge cases and examples:
- Example 1 (side-effect call): Client requests creation of a billing invoice via function-call. mode=strict-json, repair_policy=none, side_effects_allowed=true. Model returns malformed JSON -> runtime returns parse_error to caller (no repair). This preserves safety for side effects.

- Example 2 (metadata extraction): mode=permissive-json, repair_policy=minimal, side_effects_allowed=false. Model returns markdown with JSON code-fence. Runtime strips fences and extracts JSON blob, validates, and returns with runtime_hook.repaired=true and repair_steps=["strip_code_fence","extract_first_json"]. Response is cached.

- Example 3 (streaming long table): mode=incremental-json, schema_ref=table-v1. Runtime performs prefix incremental-parse; when partial chunk looks invalid, it buffers up to x ms before attempting local reassembly; if still invalid, write partial error event to trace and continue streaming with a best-effort JSON chunk flagged as partial. Final validation at stream close triggers a revalidate job; if final validation fails and side_effects_allowed=true, runtime emits error and aborts any downstream function-call.

Lifecycle and idempotency rules for function-calling hooks:
- If a function-call will trigger an external side-effect, runtime must mark the call as "guarded". Guarded calls can be executed only after: (a) strict validation succeeded, and (b) a request-unique transaction token has been minted and stored in the request trace.
- Retries must be idempotent: if caller enables retry semantics, runtime should ensure either the function-call is idempotent or the runtime performs a dry-run validation without committing side-effects on retries until an explicit confirmation step.

Operational and telemetry needs:
- Capture counters for parse_failures, repairs_applied, repair_confidence_distribution, cache_hit_by_mode, side_effect_guard_rejections.
- Sample full repaired payloads into a secure sampling bucket for offline triage. Include the prompt, model config, kernel id, and schema_ref in the sample metadata.

Open questions and TODOs:
- Schema evolution: how do we map schema id versions to cached entries efficiently? Proposal: embed schema id + version hash into cache key and allow a mapping table for backward-compatible schemas in the control plane.
- Repair audit retention: how long do we keep repair metadata in cached entries? Recommend 30 days by default, configurable per-tenant.
- Performance: run a perf experiment measuring median p99 extra CPU time for minimal repairs at 8k context size across top 3 kernels.

Action items:
- Omar: prototype minimal-repair library in runtime post-processing (PR referenced above).
- Lena: update scheduler to expose priority hints and CPU worker pool metrics (ENG-1423).
- Diego: add telemetry counters and a tracing span that captures repair steps.
- Maya: draft proposal for schema caching semantics (follow-up doc).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft. Looking for feedback specifically on safe caching invariants and whether the repair policy taxonomy is sufficient for most experiments. Also would like concrete suggestions for examples of minimal repairs beyond the set enumerated above.
